opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's one of those books that changed how I see almost everything around me, including myself.

Bourdieu's core argument is that taste isn't really personal. We like to think that what music we listen to, what food we enjoy, how we decorate our homes, even what we find funny, comes from some authentic inner self. But he shows, with a huge amount of survey data from 1960s France, that taste maps very closely onto class position, and specifically onto the combination of economic capital and what he calls cultural capital: your education, your family background, the things you absorbed growing up without even noticing.

The part that really hit me is the idea that taste works as a way of drawing boundaries. When someone says "that's tacky" or "that's so pretentious," they're not just making an aesthetic judgment. They're placing themselves in a social hierarchy and placing other people below or apart from them. Taste classifies, and it classifies the classifier. I think that line stayed with me more than anything else.

Why did it influence my life? A few reasons.

First, it made me more humble about my own preferences. There were things I was quietly proud of liking, and I realized a lot of that was just my upbringing and my education speaking, plus a bit of wanting to signal that I belonged to a certain group. That's uncomfortable to admit, but it's freeing too. You stop treating your taste as a moral achievement.

Second, it gave me a lens for understanding people and markets. If you work on products, or think about consumers, or about why certain brands suddenly become cool and then uncool, Bourdieu explains a lot. The elite constantly move away from whatever becomes popular, because once something is widely accessible, it no longer works as a marker of distinction. You can see this cycle everywhere: in fashion, in coffee, in travel, even in which apps people say they use.

Third, it helped me understand mobility, people moving between classes or between countries. When you move into a new environment, you often feel this subtle awkwardness that isn't about money at all. It's about not knowing the codes: what to order, how to talk about art, what counts as a respectable hobby. Bourdieu calls this habitus, the embodied dispositions you carry with you. Reading him, I felt like someone had finally named an experience I'd had but couldn't articulate.

It's not an easy book. It's long, dense, and very French in its style. But I'd recommend it to anyone who wants to see the invisible rules of social life. After you read it, you can't really go to a dinner party, or walk into a store, or scroll through social media the same way again.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I first read Bourdieu's Distinction when I was in my twenties, and honestly, it was uncomfortable. The book basically tells you that your taste isn't really yours. What you like to eat, the music you find moving, the way you decorate your apartment, whether you think a film is "deep" or "pretentious" — all of that is shaped by where you come from, how much cultural capital your family had, what kind of schooling you got. Bourdieu's famous line is that taste classifies, and it classifies the classifier. When you say "I don't like that, it's vulgar," you're not just describing the object. You're placing yourself in a social hierarchy.

For me that was a bit of a shock, because I grew up thinking of taste as the most personal thing about me. It felt like the part of my identity that I had chosen. And then here comes this French sociologist with hundreds of pages of survey data showing that my "choices" are statistically predictable from my parents' occupations.

But the reason I recommend it is not that it made me cynical. It actually did the opposite. Once you see that taste is socially constructed, two things happen. First, you become much more generous toward people whose preferences are different from yours. The person who likes things you find tacky isn't lacking something. They're just playing a different game, with a different history. That changed how I treat people, in business and in life.

Second, you start to notice the mechanism in real time. In China, especially over the last twenty years, you can watch distinction being manufactured almost month by month. Specialty coffee, camping, certain brands, certain ways of talking about art. A lot of what we call consumption upgrading is really people trying to acquire the signals of a class they want to belong to. If you work in consumer products, or media, or investing, that is the most important thing to understand. People are not buying the object. They're buying a position.

And finally, the book gave me a kind of freedom. If my taste was given to me, then I'm allowed to question it. I can ask, do I actually enjoy this, or do I enjoy being the kind of person who enjoys this? Sometimes the answer is embarrassing. But asking the question honestly is, I think, where real taste starts. So it's a book that took something away from me and then gave back something better.

astra-6.text:
I’d recommend it because it changed how I understand taste—including my own. We tend to think that the music we love, the food we enjoy, or the art we appreciate reflects something very personal. Bourdieu asks us to consider how those preferences are shaped by our upbringing, education, and social position.

What really stayed with me was the idea that taste also draws boundaries. When we call something sophisticated or vulgar, we’re often making a judgment about the people who enjoy it, too. That made me more reflective about my own judgments. Why do I admire this? Why am I dismissing that? Is it actually about the thing itself, or about what liking it says about me?

For me, the value of the book is that it makes those everyday assumptions visible. You can still enjoy what you enjoy, but perhaps with a little less certainty that your taste makes you superior to somebody else.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d recommend it because it changed how I think about taste. We often treat our preferences—in food, music, art, even how we dress—as very personal expressions of who we are. Bourdieu asks us to look at how those preferences are shaped by our upbringing, education, and social position, and how they become ways of signaling belonging or drawing boundaries.

For me, the powerful question is: when I say something is “good,” am I describing what I enjoy, or am I repeating a standard I’ve learned to associate with status? That doesn’t make the enjoyment fake. But it does make me more curious about my own judgments, and less quick to dismiss someone else’s.

That’s why I’d recommend it. It gives you a way to examine things that feel so natural you rarely think to question them.
